summary: For pupils aged 12–13, this is a working-scientifically (procedural) goal: plan and carry out force investigations — measuring force with a newton meter, investigating the force–extension relationship (Hooke's Law), and collecting motion data to test Newton's Second Law. The craft to be learned is variable control (independent = force applied, dependent = extension, control = the same spring), accurate measurement of EXTENSION (increase in length, not total length), repeating readings, and turning real, scattered data into a force–extension graph with a line of best fit. At this level, stop short of the spring-constant equation (F = ke) and gradient calculation (those are later GCSE content); focus on the proportional relationship (a straight line through the origin), the limit of proportionality where it bends, and careful measurement and graphing. The strongest learning combines a hands-on practical with real apparatus and a graph-building task that confronts the best-fit misconception as scatter appears.
misconceptions: The line of best fit must pass through every data point (Oak-named graphing misconception) — antidote: have pupils invent plots with small measurement errors so the line is seen to average scatter
Measuring the spring's total length instead of its extension
Recording force in grams/kilograms rather than newtons; treating mass as if it were a force
Changing more than one variable, or not repeating readings
Assuming proportionality continues forever — ignoring the limit of proportionality
Describing the pattern as 'the length doubles per newton' rather than 'the same extension is added per newton'

activities.title: Hooke's Law practical with real apparatus
steps: Clamp a spring, measure and record its natural (unstretched) length first.
State the variables before starting: independent = force applied (added in equal steps), dependent = extension, control = the same spring throughout.
Add weight one equal step at a time (hang slotted masses and convert to weight using W = m × g, or read force directly in newtons from a newton meter), letting the spring settle each time.
Measure the new length at each load and read the ruler squarely — line your eye level with the mark, or use a set square against the ruler to avoid parallax error.
Calculate extension at each step: extension = current length − natural length.
Repeat each reading (and read again on unloading) and take a mean, so scatter and anomalies become visible.
Record force in newtons and extension in a results table.
activities.insight: Force is measured in newtons; extension (not total length) is the quantity that responds to force; controlling variables and repeating readings is what makes the relationship trustworthy.

activities.title: Plotting force vs extension and drawing a line of best fit
steps: Plot Force (newtons) on the y-axis against Extension on the x-axis using your recorded data.
Draw a single straight line of best fit through the scattered points — do NOT join the dots point-to-point; aim for a line with roughly equal numbers of points on each side.

Describe the pattern in words: up to the limit of proportionality, equal steps of force add the SAME extension each time (not 'the length doubles'), and with zero extension at zero force this means extension is directly proportional to force — a straight line through the origin.
Continue adding load in a second investigation (or extend the dataset) until the once-straight line starts to bend, and mark that point where proportionality ends — the limit of proportionality.

Separately, note that if the spring is loaded past its elastic limit (which for many springs is at or only a little beyond the limit of proportionality) it may be permanently stretched and no longer return to its natural length; this is a distinct idea from the limit of proportionality.
Explain why the line is drawn to average scatter rather than connecting every point.
activities.insight: A best-fit line averages real measurement scatter rather than connecting individual points; the force–extension relationship is proportional only up to a limit of proportionality, after which it bends (and, at still greater loads beyond the elastic limit, the spring may deform permanently).

activities.title: Testing Newton's Second Law with a trolley
steps: Apply a measured force to a trolley of known mass (include a risk assessment for any hanging masses).
State the trolley's starting condition (e.g. starting from rest) before describing how its motion changes.

Calculate the predicted acceleration using a = F / m, where F is the applied (driving) force and m is the total mass being accelerated (the trolley plus any hanging masses that move with it), assuming friction is small.
Measure the trolley's actual acceleration (e.g. with light gates or a motion sensor/data logger) and compare it with the calculated acceleration.
Discuss sources of difference (e.g. friction opposing the applied force, measurement error) between prediction and observation.
activities.insight: A measured applied force on a known total moving mass (trolley plus any hanging masses) predicts an acceleration via a = F/m when friction is small; more precisely, it is the resultant force (applied force minus friction) that determines acceleration — a change in motion, not an instant speed or direction. Because real friction makes the resultant smaller than the applied force, the observed acceleration is usually a little below F/m, and comparing prediction with real motion tests Newton's Second Law.

activities.title: Plan and reason about the method (companion check)
steps: Put the method steps in the correct order: plan the variables, measure natural length, add load in equal steps, measure new length, calculate extension, repeat readings, plot, draw best-fit line, identify the limit of proportionality.
Identify which quantity is the independent variable, dependent variable, and control variable for the spring investigation.
Given a graph with scattered points, select or sketch the correct line of best fit (not the dot-to-dot line).
Given a force–extension graph that curves, mark the limit of proportionality.
activities.insight: Secure procedural reasoning — correct sequencing, variable identification, best-fit choice, and recognising the limit of proportionality — underpins a trustworthy investigation.

checkQuestion: Here is a spring clamped at the top, a set of identical slotted masses, a ruler, and a newton meter. Investigate how the stretching force affects the spring's extension (Hooke's Law). Plan and carry out the investigation, record your results, plot a graph, and tell me what your graph shows about the relationship — including where, if anywhere, it stops being proportional.
checkAnswer: Measures the spring's natural length, adds masses one at a time, records the force (weight of the masses, or from the newton meter) and the EXTENSION (new length minus natural length) at each step, repeating readings; plots force (or mass) against extension; draws a BEST-FIT straight line through the scattered points (not dot-to-dot), showing extension proportional to force; identifies the limit of proportionality where the line starts to curve. Controls variables (same spring, measures extension not total length).
